review:
Игра лютая дерьмятина. Абсолютно убогий геймдизайн. Тебя заставляют проходить игру именно так, как задумал разработчик, и никак иначе.

Особенно вводит в заблуждение трейлер, который показывает, как весело можно играться с магическим набором способностей. Но по факту тебя постоянно держат в жестких рамках, а любое отступление от задуманного пути игра наказывает.

Решил поубивать стражников? Минус испытание.
Хочешь подольше остаться на локации? Минус испытание.

И вот тут начинается самое веселое. За эти испытания какой то "гений" решил выдавать очки прокачки. То есть я не могу проходить игру так, как мне нравится. Я обязан играть строго по заданным правилам, иначе просто ослабляю самого себя.

Да, испытания можно перепроходить. Только вот за один заход закрыть их все невозможно, поэтому каждый уровень приходится проходить по 2 или 3 раза. И это вообще не весело.

Ну и вишенка на торте это чудесный нарратив. Каждый раз видеть диалоги формата:

"Ты собираешься поджечь этот фитиль?"
"О да! Я собираюсь поджечь этот фитиль!"
"Давай уже, поджигай этот фитиль!"

Просто нет слов.

Вот серьезно, пожелание всем разработчикам таких игр. Не надо фиксированно показывать подобные диалоги при каждом перепрохождении уровня. Один раз показали и дальше скрыли. Потому что выглядит это настолько паршиво, что уже глаз дергается, когда приходится снова запускать уровень.

Короче, игра совершенно не оправдывает ожиданий. Очередная поделка с отвратительным дизайном. Брать стоит только если вообще больше не во что играть.

Очень прикольный двухмерный стелс-платформер c использованием стихийной магии в своей геймплейной основе. У героя есть огненные способности (метание файерболов для поджигания предметов и дыма для ослепления врагов, а также кратковременный взлёт на огненно-пердильной тяге), водные (заморозка, создание небольших ледяных кубов или пузыря для полёта) и земляные (лозы для вскарабкивания или опутывания NPC, трава для пряток, парашют при пикировании вниз). Причём чтобы что-то сотворить, конкретную стихию сначала нужно взять из окружающего мира — факелов/костров, водоёмов/снега, травы/кустарников. И всё эти навыки, конечно, не сразу даются, а по мере прохождения, более того — замаксить их полностью можно лишь на НГ++. Под финал первого прохождения также прокачиваются довольно имбовые вещи типа живой воды или телепорта при помощи растения в заранее заготовленную точку. Ещё с собой можно носить осколки метеорита с разными пассивными абилками — аналог костяных амулетов из Dishonored, максимум 3 штуки одновременно.

В Wildfire используется системный подход, когда все механики взаимосвязаны и окружение реагирует на твои действия: всё, что горит, можно поджечь, горящее — тушить, а мёртвое (людей, животных или флору) — оживить; на льду враг подскользнётся, от бегущей горящей курицы словит панику, а если поймать его в пузырь и запустить в небо, то разобьётся о поверхность при падении. В общем, как проходить небольшие уровни и решать поставленные перед ним задачи — игрок решает исходя из имеющихся у него на данный момент возможностей и собственной смекалки. Хотя мочить всех и вся, особенно в первое прохождение, будет трудно: главный персонаж слаб и лишается жизни-сердечка с одной вражеской тычки, прямых боевых абилок у него нет (убийственная комбинация «опутать лозами и поджечь» станет доступна лишь во второй половине игры), к тому же доп. очки для прокачки тут дают за пацифизм и незаметность, а не рубилово (хотя никто и не запрещает) — это всё-таки стелс как-никак. Поэтому придётся тихо сидеть в траве, поменьше шуметь при перемещении и юзать стихии для отвлечения/стана/паники врагов. А вот уже на НГ+, обладая почти полным магическим инструментарием, можно и повеселиться, попутно выполняя различные условия на уровнях для 100% — тут реально интересно выполнять ачивки, что обычно редкость в играх. Уж на что я не люблю спидраны — всё равно с удовольствием потел и пытался придумать, как пролететь уровень за 1,5 минуты вместо стандартных 20 с прятками в кустах и обходом врагов.

Короче, Wildfire точно понравится тем, кто любит игры за широту геймплейных возможностей и кому не чужды стелс-элементы.

Criminally underrated stealth action side-scroller with immersive sim elements. The design is quite genius the way it encourages you to replay levels to complete optional objectives, like no kills or no reloads. Pairing a few objectives together make interesting choices and challenges for each run. 

The interaction between systems has lots of room for chaos where even failure is fun and recoverable. The story and art are serviceable, but not absolutely stellar. However, the graphics  are mostly very readable and have their own charm. Co-op is nearly seamless and adds to the experience, though the slower pace and puzzle elements might not be for every player. 

The only issue I had was the save system, where selecting 'new game' instantly deleted my progress without even a confirmation screen. 

Big recommend for stealth fans. I hope the studio does more in the future, I'll keep an eye out.

Wildfire is a 2D side-scrolling stealth game with immersive sim elements. You play as a witch using elemental magic (fire, water and earth) to sneak past guards in order to rescue your kidnapped villagers. The plot does a decent job of motivating you forward, along with having a nice little twist at the end. But the gameplay is the real highlight of the experience. You are rewarded for finding clever uses for your abilities to circumvent obstacles. For example, you can use fire to burn a nearby thicket to cause the guards to panic and run away, giving you the chance to sneak past. However, doing so may risk you getting hurt in the fire, as well as removing said bush as a potential hiding spot. Instead, you might turn the fireball into smoke, stunning a guard for long enough to get past anyway. Or using the fire to give your jump a rocket boost, allowing you to soar over the obstacle. And this is not getting into what you can do with water or earth. Each level has multiple ways to complete its objectives, rewarding experimentation with badass moments.

In addition, each level has multiple objectives, completing each of which earns you ability points to upgrade your character. These bonus objectives include completing an extra, harder objective, finishing under a certain time limit, rescuing all imprisoned villagers in a level, avoiding detection or killing anyone, etc. They do not need to be completed in a single run, allowing you to focus on certain objectives per play through and encouraging you to replay the level multiple times. There are also more skills and passive boons that there are opportunities to collect them, encouraging players to dip into New Game+.

The game controls very smoothly, with fluid movement and clear indication of when you are hidden, where your projectile is aimed at, and what will happen when it reaches its destination. I did encounter a few bugs, most notably in the level where you save your imprisoned lynx, but the majority of the game had no issues. I did not like menu navigation, I needed to use the escape key a lot to move between menu’s and often felt trapped within them.

Graphically, praise must be given to the legibility of the pixel art on display. While it is not the more stunning pixel artwork in gaming, you are never in any doubt as to what objects in the world are intractable and which ones aren’t. Good use of colour also helps with highlighting objects of note. In a late game level, you come across a fountain with flowing blue water. The game's art direction makes it clear that this is a source of water, and not just a bit of set dressing. The sound design is also great, giving good feedback for things such  as where guards are in your proximity.

The game felt great to play, plus all the bonus objectives and robust New Game+ mode gives this game plenty of replayability. The immersive sim elements work excellently with the stealth gameplay, leading to plenty of cool moments.

[h1]Fun, little gem of a stealth-like platformer with elemental interactions that could benefit from a level editor[/h1]

[b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] is a delightful stealth game centered around elemental interactions, reminiscent of titles like [i]Noita[/i] and [i]Magicka[/i]. In this game, you play as a newly awakened witch who harnesses the power of three elements: fire, water, and earth (grass), with skills that unlock as you progress.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The core mechanic of [b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] is its elemental interaction system, which operates on basic physics. You can burn grass and melt ice as you walk through them with a fire spell (or when your body is ablaze). Objects and enemies can be set afloat with water bubbles, and forest fires can be extended by throwing grass and vines. Discovering these combinations is a joy, and even after 10 hours in, I'm still finding new ways elements interact with each other.

Though [b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] fashions itself as a platformer stealth game, it is fundamentally a platformer puzzle game. Enemies and the environment are obstacles to be solved rather than simply combated, especially considering the only ways to kill them is through fall damage or high temperature. You can choose to run and gun or stealthily navigate through levels. Each level offers objectives that sometimes require abandoning stealth for a more direct approach, especially during speed runs.

The game also supports coop, which doubles the fun as you and a friend experiment with elemental magic together.

[h1]The Less than Good[/h1]

But what about the negative reviews?

They seem to stem from players who aim to obsessively complete all objectives in a single run. Many objectives are optional, and fortunately, you can revisit levels to complete specific objectives without redoing everything. 

[b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] encourages trial and error, much like other puzzle games, making each run a chance to try something new. That said, I understand the frustration of objectives being tied to skill points, as they are needed to unlock new abilities and there are no other means to progress.

Where [b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] falls short is in its approach to extending game duration. The current system relies on players redoing levels for perfect scores, which can become repetitive. The addition of a level editor would greatly enhance the game, allowing for player-created levels and extending its replay value. This would offer endless opportunities for creativity and new ways to figure out elemental interactions.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

With a price less than 10 USD (2 USD during Summer Sale 2024), [b][i]Wildfire[/i][/b] is a fun, little gem that you can enjoy solo or with a friend - a delightful experience worth revisiting once in a while.

It's one of those games that has the same mechanic that they had to take out of Assassin's Creed because it was so unpopular. Perfect-run the task at hand in just the right way and you get the rewards, fail on any of the objectives and you get a big red X instead.

It's actually kind of worse here, because rather than just trying to sync with Ezio's historic actions, you're playing for upgrade points that enhance your abilities, so you really are losing out on something tangible with those red X's. In addition, the game punishes you for mistakes by having a "No reloads" objective which you can only clear if you replay the level from the start each time, which gets kind of tedious.

Am well aware that you don't *have* to get all the upgrade points and can probably steam through the game and come back later to replay all the levels that it considers that you botched, but that kind of feels like forced longevity, and I just can't see myself wanting to play through it a second time.

To be fair, without the panel-of-judges mechanic the game isn't bad at all; It's a just shame that it railroads you away from having fun with it.

Wildfire is a 2D stealth game in a fantasy setting. Reminiscent of Oddworld, you have villagers you can save in most levels. While I like the lighting system in Mark of the Ninja, Wildfire honestly feels like the better stealth game as well as the better representation of what can be done in 2D platforming.

The side-quests ranged from fair to impossible when I began the game. But as I progressed, I unlocked more and more abilities relating to the four elements - you unlock fire, water, earth and air in that order, as well as having spirit abilities from the beginning - that opened up completely new ways to play the game. This made going back to earlier levels to achieve what once felt impossible a lot of fun. So if you're struggling with an optional quest, you can always move along and come back to it later.

Replayability is built into this game through the optional quests, such as ghost, no reloads, speed runs, etc. I can see players finding new and interesting ways to make the game more challenging once mastering the quests. The game is very immersive and it is easy to lose track of time.

The graphics are cute little sprites, reminiscent of 16-bit console games, and despite it not holding your hand like Mark of the Ninja, even though there are only a couple of rudimentary indications as to how well hidden you are and whether or not the enemy can see or hear you, you're never unsure. The controls for keyboard and mouse are nice and simple - like a lot of platform games, the jumping takes a little getting used to, but other than that the controls are fine.

TLDR - Wildfire is very replayable and quite cheap to buy. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who is a fan of stealth games, especially 2D stealth games like Oddworld and Mark of the Ninja, and give it a rating of eight or nine out of ten.

This is a very tepid recommendation. It's a very casual puzzle platformer (not an im-sim lmao) that only gets easier the longer you play. It's enjoyable enough. There's nothing particularly wrong with it, though I encountered dozens of bugs in my time with the game.

There are only about 26 stages with one boss stage. In order to unlock all of the powers and upgrades, you need to go into at least NG+, if not NG++. By that point, you can practically finish the levels in your sleep, and you'll get more fun from trolling NPCs than finishing the objectives. I feel like more could've been done with the concepts and mechanics, though. There's still a lot of meat on these bones. Challenge stages would've been nice. A sequel is definitely an option, given the ending of the game. The ability to combine powers seems like an obvious angle that the game doesn't even consider. I'll just say that it's good the game isn't expensive.

Other than those things, there are a bunch of quibbles that they could fix with a polished-up sequel (or a patch to this game): going to NG+ resets all of your settings, some stages have unskippable story segments after them that you have to sit through every time you finish the stage... which you will be doing to collect upgrade points, you sometimes have to fight with the controls to get the game to let you do what you want (not as big of a deal as it sounds)... a variety of other things like that. It's a game that could use more polish.

I have finished this game twice fully and only have the boss stage left on the third run. I mainly replayed to collect achievements and see what a fully-upgraded character plays like. By the end of your first playthrough, you will have seen basically everything this game has to offer. Your replay value will vary. Note that two achievements are locked behind co-op, which I did not touch and will be the only achievements I haven't collected. No idea why game companies continue to lock achievements behind multiplayer, but there it is.
